title: Bijapur Sultanate
capsule: The Bijapur Sultanate (Adil Shahi dynasty) was one of the five Deccan successor states that emerged from the fragmentation of the Bahmani Sultanate, formally independent from 1490 under Yusuf Adil Shah. It reached its territorial and cultural apex under Ali Adil Shah II (r. 1656–1672), when the Gol Gumbaz mausoleum — one of the largest domed structures in the world — was completed, and Bijapur's court produced distinguished Deccani miniature painting and Urdu literature. The sultanate was weakened by Maratha pressure under Shivaji, who seized key forts including Purandar (1665) by treaty, and was finally extinguished in 1686 when the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb captured Bijapur city after an 18-month siege.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Bijapur Sultanate's territories are documented through Mughal administrative records, Deccan chronicles, and Portuguese treaty documents; the extent of fluctuating frontier districts with Ahmadnagar and Golkonda is reconstructed from campaign accounts and is somewhat approximate.
